column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check

The article names the Sikh ruler approached after Dubba as Maharaja Ranjeet Singh, who died in 1839; the name was left out. The article's casualty section lists Mir Nasir Khan Talpur among the fallen Amirs while its battle section has him escape to Hyderabad Fort; the list was left out. Troop and casualty figures in the article conflict (2,800 vs 8,000-10,000 British; 5,000 or 6,000 Talpur dead; 256 or 27 or 3,000 British): given as disputed.
Roman numbers differ between the article's narrative (10,000) and Otto of Sankt Blasien (30,000); both attributed.
The article has the king watching the battle from Bassenbourg Hill across the river; the entry says the other army withdrew on hearing of the defeat. The hill was left out.
The article calls the earlier northern defeat Mihmandoost; the entry calls it Damghan (the same campaign). The name was left out to avoid seeming to disagree.
The article says that after the envoys' deaths Narathihapate 'gained confidence that the Yuan would attack him', probably a slip for 'would not'; left out.

The article gives the Spanish army as 25,000 when gathered and 'more than 13,000' at the battle, and says the Franco-Navarrese were outnumbered 2 to 1; the figures were left out and the odds given only as 'heavily outnumbered'.
SKIPPED: article under 300 words, about 200 beyond what the entry already says
The article calls the Bijapur ruler both Adil Khan and Adil Shah and the captain Salabut and Salabat Khan; spelled as in the battle section.
The article numbers the emperor Lothair II, the entry Lothair III (the same man); the number was left out.

SKIPPED: article about 300 words, much of it already in the entry; it also says the confederates could not besiege Zurich and withdrew, while the entry says they besieged it (the entry may need checking)

The article has Nobunaga himself joining the army and ordering the charge and the retreat; the entry says the army was sent by Nobunaga under Shibata Katsuie. Nobunaga's presence was left out. The article spells the river both Tetori and Tedori.
The article gives Irish losses only from English reports (200 to 300), likely an overestimate; left out. Red Hugh O'Donnell's part is in the entry; the article quotes only the Annals.
SKIPPED: article about 300 words, most of it already in the entry
The article calls the battle indecisive and says some sources credit either side with victory; the entry says the Saadi army checked the invaders. No verdict was given.
The article says the available sources give different dates for the battle; the entry's 21 February 1543 was kept and no other date given.
The article calls Al-Ashraf commander of the Mamluk army; he was an Ayyubid, so 'Mamluk' was left out.
Climate figures (temperatures, sunshine hours, a 48 °C reading) left out as padding. The article's 'force 6.5' for the 1799 earthquake left out (unclear scale).

Death year: the article gives 1803–1869 and says he died a year after settling in Damascus in June 1868; the entry gives 1868. Death year left out. Article also says the Assyrian massacres were perpetrated by the triple alliance in 1843 and 1846; consistent with entry.

Death: the article gives 1308 (and Sargis II's rule from 1308); the entry gives d. c. 1306. Both the death year and the end of his rule left out. The law code named in the entry is not in the article.

The article states the 1914 dahir's sponsors viewed Arab urban Islamic law as despotic and describes Berber penal customs; left out as one-sided wording. The article says Muhammad V signed 'under no duress'; given only as the fact that he signed.
Article describes him as a proponent of independence from the Kingdom as well; the entry speaks of separation from the Antilles. Both are compatible. His sons' present-day offices left out.

Nyatapola: the article says it was built in six months, late 1702 to early 1703; the entry says 1702. Year left out. The article's 'In 1914' treaty with Kantipur and Lalitpur is an evident slip and was left out. Article says the plague ran 1716–1722 in one heading and 1716 to 1723 in the text; end year left out.
Article calls Niccolò III's 1393 accession 'to the Ferrarese duchy'; Ferrara became a duchy later, so written as 'ruler of Ferrara'.
The Akyem states named in the entry do not appear in the article. Ghana's ranking as a gold producer and present-day production figures left out.
The treachery by which the entry says he was seized is not in the article; not mentioned either way.
Present-day employment and unemployment figures (2017, 2021) and the opposition leaders' remarks left out to avoid present-day assessments.

The article cites other accounts that Sultan Agung's forces conquered Blambangan in 1639; the entry says it resisted his campaigns in the 1630s. The 1639 conquest is left out. The VOC control of 1767–1772 named in the entry is not in the excerpt.
SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance and adds little to the description (Matthias's entente with the Turks, Prague never taken, the 1490 succession)

The article dates Jipsa's arrival to the eighth year of Emperor Tenji and gives 676, which do not agree; left out. The article says Pung killed Boksin; the Nihon Shoki excerpt has him beheaded on Pung's order. Both consistent with the entry.
SKIPPED: article under 300 words, partly garbled, and adds little beyond the description (Rígsthula, sailors and traders, the Icelandic goði)
Article: 462 men, 30 women and 2 children; entry: some 500 of his men. Compatible. The article does not say when he took the name Arthur Holmston, only 'later'; worded loosely.

The entry dates the rush from 1693; the article dates Borba Gato's find to 1695 and says it led to the rush. Written as 'among the early finds' to avoid a contradiction. Diamond finds after 1729 (entry) are not in the article. The 1720 convoy and others' losses and the superlative claims (longest gold rush, most populous city of Latin America) left out.

The entry says it won every elected seat in the 1962 elections to the Legislative Council; the article gives 54 of 55 district council seats, the remaining councillor joining the party a week later, with 16 of the 55 going on to the 33-member LegCo. Seat counts and LegCo detail left out; written as an overwhelming victory. A reviewer may wish to check the entry. Present-day state of emergency and LegCo changes left out.
The article's 'Irish and Greek ancestry' is legendary genealogy and is told as such.
SKIPPED: article under 250 words; adds only his deposition in 1511 and retirement to Samarkand. It also dates his accession to 1474 or 1480, against the entry's c. 1480

The article contradicts itself on location: its lead places the city on the Vardar and also near Knezhje (Sveti Nikole), and a later passage calls the Knezhje identification a fabrication that moved the city inland from the Axius. The entry has 'on the Vardar near modern Sveti Nikole'; neither the river nor the dispute's direction is pressed. The 2008 finds are dated in the article to the 6th–3rd century BC; the entry speaks of Hellenistic buildings. Dates left out.

The entry says the city was capital of Mauretania Caesariensis after 42 CE; the article has Claudius dividing the kingdom in 44 AD after a four-year revolt (and repeats 44 AD). The year of the division is left out. The article's paragraph on Juba II and the division of Numidia is confused (33 BC, unrest 26-20 BC); only the plain facts of his upbringing and the rebuilding were used. The titular-see list in the article belongs to Caesarea in Numidia, a different city: not used.

The article's sections on literature, prominent families and present-day descendants (2004 estimate of 300,000-500,000) were left out. The mission population figure is the article's for the mission Indigenous Californian population.
SKIPPED: article of about 330 words, nearly all of it already in the entry's description

The article gives no year for his return to Chile (the entry says 1822); none is printed. The article names the Order of Ministros de los Enfermos Agonizantes de San Camilo de Lelis; shortened to 'the order known as the Buena Muerte'.

The article quotes Margaret Plant for a domination 'from 1337 to 1405' and also says the family ousted the della Scala in 1338, while its lead and the entry give lordship from 1318; Plant's dates were not used. The article says Marsilio, one of Francesco Novello's sons, died soon after 1406, but its list of members gives a Marsilio who died in 1435; he is left out.
The article gives his birth as c. 1261/62, consistent with the entry's c. 1261; not repeated. Długosz's account is quoted in the article; it is attributed to him in the text.

The entry says Despina Khatun was the aunt of Zeno's wife; the article says his wife was said to be a relative of Theodora Despina but that their relationship and degree of kinship are uncertain and unproven. The kinship is left out of the text. The article names the King of Poland as Casimir II, which cannot be right for 1474 (Casimir IV reigned then); the king is left unnamed. The article says Zeno was 'nephew of Doge Michele Morosini', ambiguous as written; left out.

The article spells the catholicos who moved to Gelati both Eudemos I (Chkheidze) and Eudemios I Chkhetidze (1557-1578) in its list; the family name is left out. The article's lead dates independent functioning from the 1470s; the text keeps to its history section's wording.

The article says the five were convicted by a military commission and also that the military brought them to the capital 'in March'; the text follows the hanging date only. The year of Whitman's return (the year after 1842) is given as 'the following year', as in the article.

The article calls his 1902 post acting-Viceroy of Sichuan; the entry's 'governor-general of Sichuan' is not contradicted. The article says the Guangzhou military government was replaced by Sun's Nationalist government in 1920; the entry says it collapsed. The text says only that he retired in 1920.

The article gives no year for the forming of Vindhya Pradesh and Madhya Bharat (the entry says 1948); none is printed. The article is mostly lists of states; the text gives the agency's structure and the main dates only.

The article spells the Munster king both Fedelmid and Feidlimid mac Crimthainn; 'Fedelmid' used. The killing of Echtigern mac Guaire in 853 and the Fragmentary Annals' drunkenness anecdote were left out for length. The article says Cerball came to prominence after 847 but also that he succeeded in 842, as the entry has it; both kept in that order.
Short article (about 300 words of substance); the text is close to the lower length. The article spells the successor Yax Nuun Ahiin I, the entry Yax Nuun Ayiin I; he is not named here.

The article names the Viceroy as 'Lord Wellington' (presumably Lord Willingdon); the Viceroy is left unnamed. The article gives the loss on cancellation of the privy purse as '1.8 million (per year)' with no currency; left out. The year of the Temple Entry Proclamation is not in the excerpt; the entry's 1936 is not contradicted.

The article contradicts itself on the dynasty's end: it rules 'c. 125 CE to c. 345 CE', inscriptions 'between the 260s and 340s', a 278 CE inscription, the Kadamba occupation of Banavasi 'c. 345', yet 'came to an end probably ... around 250–275 CE'; its lead says first to third centuries. The entry says 2nd-3rd century. All end dates are left out. The article's sentence on the Western Kshatrapa Prithivi-sena in 222 CE succeeding Haritiputra Siva-skanda-varman makes no sense and was not used.

The entry says the work was written in Japanese; the article says the preface and introduction are in Chinese and the five volumes mix Chinese characters and katakana. The text gives the article's description of the script, which does not deny that the language is Japanese. The article's literal title translation ('the reflect of the generations of Chūzan') is not repeated.

The article dates the Mecklenburg conquest to the early 1230s but explains Pomerania-Demmin's weakness by the Treaty of Kremmen of 1236; the treaty is left out. The article's sentence placing the Wendish Crusade 'in the following year' after 1057 is garbled; only the year 1147 is used. The entry glosses the name as 'those beyond the Peene'; the article's etymology (across + Peene + dwellers) agrees.

The entry dates the Battle of the Pass of Brander 'around 1308'; the article puts it 'three years' after 1306 and in 1309 in its castles section. No year is printed. The present chief and the death of the previous chief in February 2026 are left out (present-day detail).

The article says Ballinger sacked him in 1928 but also that he led the ICU until his resignation as national secretary in 1929; the date of his removal is left out. The article says he died in London in 1951 while also saying he stayed in East London; the place of death is left out. The entry gives c. 1896 for his birth, the article 1896; no birth year is printed.

The article dates the martyrdom only to the Diocletianic persecution; the entry's 'around 304' is not contradicted. The article says the first project was 'on the same site' as the Carpetani hill fort; 'on the hill' follows that.
The last paragraph is short (about 45 words); the article gives little more on the end of the association.

The article calls the Consistori the most ancient literary institution of the Western world and lists prestigious later members (Voltaire, Hugo, Mistral); left out as praise not attributed. The article says the academy was founded in 1323 and later restored by Clémence Isaure; this figure is not explained further and is left out.
The article does not say whether Teisamenos was the seer at the sacrifice (it writes 'Teisamenos?'); the text keeps them apart.

The article places the enlarged logging area on the Yucatan Peninsula; the entry speaks of the Bay of Honduras. Both refer to the same settlements; the text uses the article's wording without contradicting the entry. The article is short (about 280 words); the text uses nearly all of it.

The article gives the length as 395 feet (120 m) in one place and about 390 feet in another, the area as 51,309 and 51,000 square feet, and the height as 124 feet for the dome and 125 feet for the building; the text gives the width (296 feet, given twice) and the dome's 124 feet, and the area as about 51,000. The entry says the palace is a museum run by the Archaeological Survey of India and was inspired by Buckingham Palace; the article says only that it is a museum and an ASI-listed monument and does not mention Buckingham Palace. The article says the original, partly three-storey palace was destroyed by the 1897 earthquake without saying what was rebuilt; the text repeats that without interpreting it.

The article says the county originated in the tenth century and that nobles held the title of Count of Geneva from the 9th century; the entry dates the counts from the eleventh century. The text gives no century of origin and starts the house with Gerold (c. 1045), which agrees with the entry. The article calls Robert of Geneva's papacy a 'shadow papacy' and the list calls him Antipope at Avignon; the text says he was raised to a rival papacy by the French cardinals who broke with Urban VI. The article's text calls Humbert VII the husband of the heiress, while its list of counts makes him the son of Maria of Geneva, daughter of Amadeus III; the text states neither.
The article says the Muslim revolt of 1871 increased French distrust of non-Jewish Algerians; left out for length.

The article says Crínán's son Maldred of Allerdale was killed in the same battle in 1045, but also that Maldred's identity as Crínán's son is disputed; the text leaves his death out. The article calls Macbeth Crínán's nephew; left out as doubtful and unexplained.
The article gives the view count of the 2019 video (17 million); left out as a figure that changes. The article calls the first film presentation mariachi folk-kitsch; the text says only mariachi.

SKIPPED: The article has about 250 words, almost all on the present-day town (a 2021 census, royal visits, the 400th anniversary, a heritage centre and a theatre); it says nothing of the 1610 colony beyond its founding by John Guy, which the entry already gives.

The article says Cyngen had three sons and then lists four (Elisedd, Ieuaf, Aeddan, Gruffydd); the text names the four without a count. The entry says Cyngen ruled from about 808 and died under pressure from Mercia; the article gives 808 without a hedge and does not mention Mercia. The text gives 808 as the article does and says nothing of Mercia. The article is short (about 270 words); the text uses nearly all of it.

The article numbers the last lord both as Ostasio III and as Ostasio V; the text uses Ostasio III. The article lists Guido III's sons with dates out of order (Obizzo d. 1431 before Pietro d. 1404 and Aldobrandino d. 1406); the text names only three of them.

The article says King Edward II granted Thomond to Thomas de Clare in 1276; Edward II did not reign until 1307, so the king is not named. The article says Donnchad was deposed in 1063 and that some sources claim he granted the Irish crown to Pope Urban II, which it calls controversial (Urban II became pope in 1088); left out.

The entry dates the end of the Anglo-Nepalese War to 1816 and names Amar Singh Thapa's surrender in 1815; the article gives no dates for the campaign and does not name Amar Singh Thapa, so the text gives none. The entry says a monument stands in Kolkata; the article says the Ochterlony column at Calcutta has since been rededicated. Left out of the text. The entry says he later served as Resident at Delhi; the article has him appointed Resident at Delhi after the battle of Delhi in 1803 and again combined with Rajputana from 1818. The text says he became Resident after the battle without a year.

The article places the zone in the Southwest Region; the entry says south-western Ethiopia. The region's name is left out, as Ethiopia's regions have changed. The article says the Gilgel Gibe III Dam 'is being built' on the Omo between Dawro and Wolayita; left out, as its state is not dated. The article says nothing of the Dawro kingdom, Menelik II's conquest or the Halala Kella wall that the entry names.

The entry gives 34 first signatories, as the article's background does; the English text drafted by Busby speaks of the signatures of thirty-five chiefs. The text gives no count. The Waitangi Tribunal's second stage was unfinished at the last date the article gives (June 2020); not mentioned. Claudia Orange's view, close to King's, left out for length.
Living and recent members listed in the article (born after 1900) are left out. The article gives Ugolino III's death as 19572 (a typing slip); not used.

The entry says he went to Geneva on a Haudenosaunee passport; the article mentions the passport only for the London journey of 1921. The text ties the passport to 1921 without saying he used another in 1923. The article says some Haudenosaunee hold him responsible for Canada's later retaliation; left out for length.

The article says some historians hold that Dhruva revolted and seized the throne, others that the transfer from Govinda II was peaceful; the entry says he seized it. The text says only that he replaced his brother. The article cites a Dhulia grant of 779 proclaiming Dhruva emperor, which sits uneasily with the entry's (and the article's own) reign from about 780; left out. The article does not say whether Silabhattarika and Sila Mahadevi are the same woman; the text keeps them apart.

The article dates his terms as general to 150-149 BC and from 148 BC, then calls him general again in 147 BC and succeeded by Kritolaos in autumn 147 BC; the text gives only his first election in 150 BC. The entry says Diaeus took command after Critolaus' defeat; the article says after his death in office. The text says on Kritolaos' death, which fits both. The entry spells the names Diaeus and Critolaus; the article uses Diaios and Kritolaos. Last paragraph is short (about 45 words).

The article gives the act of repossession as both 12 September and 14 September 1692, and the 1692 force as both 150 soldiers and sixty soldiers with one hundred auxiliaries: no day or number used. The article does not tell his death on campaign in 1704 (in the entry), so the heading is Legacy.
The article does not mention nationalisation of industry and banks (in the entry); nothing contradicts it.
The article calls his 1812 force small yet gives 1,550 men: number left out.

Birth: the article gives c. 1657 (born 1657 at Tirah); the entry's dates are c. 1672–1728. Birth year and age left out. The Nizam's invasion is dated March 1724 in the article's lead and 23 March 1723 in its body: no year given for it.

The article says both that he was ethnically Han from both parents and that he was the son of a Muslim Hui: his ancestry is left out. The article says he 'reigned for 16 years', which matches the entry's sixteen years.
Short article (about 300 words); the text may fall near the lower limit.
The article places Qin's famine in 646 BCE and tells the invasion after it without dating the battle; the entry dates the Battle of Han to 645 BCE. No year given for the battle.

The entry says Zeta was absorbed into the Ottoman sanjak of Scutari; the article says his brother Stefan II succeeded him as a nominal Ottoman vassal and the family ceded power to the Metropolitans of Cetinje in 1516. Zeta's fate after 1496 left out. The entry dates the Oktoih to 1494; the article gives the first Oktoih as 1493/94 and the second as 1494: no year given for them.

The confirmed article is the State of East Sumatra (1947–1950), a narrower subject than the entry's region; the text keeps to what bears on the region and its history. The article spells Simalungan once and Simalungun elsewhere: Simalungun used. Possibly one for more-mismatch.tsv if the entry should link a regional article.
SKIPPED: The article has about 250 words, nearly all of them already in the entry's description; only a paragraph on the Western Depot and the Inner Branch Depot is left.
The entry's last sentence gives the older reading (a concession strengthening the landholders); the text gives both readings as the article does, attributed.
The article gives his death as 7 December 1733 in the lead and 16 November 1733 in the body, with burial on 10 December 1733: no day given.

The article calls Simon bar Giora the leader of the Sicarii outside the walls; that claim is left out. The article has the Zealots seizing the Temple in 67; the entry says his faction held the inner court from 68. No year given for the seizure.
SKIPPED: The article has under 200 words of substance, most of them already in the entry (the pillar, its inscription, the reclaimed land).

The article gives his death as 25 March 1920 in the lead and 23 March in the body: no day given. His birthplace is spelled Wegwitz in the lead and Wegnitz in the body: the place is named only by its district. The article dates his post as inspector general from 1900 in the lead and 1904 in the body: left out.
Short article (about 290 words); the text may fall near the lower limit. 'Discovery and study' is a heading of the object list, used here for the excavation.

The entry says Eppillus appears to have ruled at Calleva Atrebatum; the article says his capital was Noviomagus Reginorum (Chichester) in the south of the kingdom while Tincomarus ruled from Calleva Atrebatum (Silchester) in the north. Neither capital is named in the text. The article gives 20 BC and 7 AD / 15 AD / 47 AD; written here as BCE/CE.

The entry says the Reich government sent troops into Saxony; the article does not mention troops, so the text says nothing about them. The article says Ebert deposed him under Article 48; the entry's 'removed him by decree' is consistent with that.
The article calls him administrator of the prince-bishopric; the entry's 'last Lutheran bishop' is kept as it stands. The entry's 'Brandenburg Pomerania' is the article's Farther Pomerania.
The article is loosely written and in places unclear (on trading diasporas, capitulations); only its clearer statements were used.
Left out garbled passages of the article: the 'Catfish' and 'Lions', the 'Ottawa Prison', and a rebellion in 1858 said to be against Falcón, Zamora's brother-in-law and fellow Federalist.

The article dates his death both 'after 1063, probably in the 1070s' and 'probably soon after' the Baghdad mission; the text gives no date. The article's succession date is unclear ('Four years later' after 1037 or 1041); the text gives no year for the succession, leaving the entry's 1041. The article is ambiguous about who captured Abarquh in 1044; left out.

The article uses Finnic in the broad Finno-Ugric sense (Mordvins, Mari, Udmurts, Komis); the entry calls them Uralic-speaking, which is consistent. Population figures for the smaller peoples were left out to avoid a list of present-day numbers; Finns and Estonians kept as rounded figures.

The article calls Govind Rai 'the ruler of Delhi', while the entry calls Prithviraj 'king of Ajmer and Delhi'. The text does not call Govind Rai ruler of Delhi. The article's lead says the garrison kept the Rajputs at bay for thirteen months; the body says Prithviraj captured the fort before the second battle. Both kept, as they agree.

The article's lead gives the defeat by Vijayanagara as 1419; its body (and the entry) give 1420 for Pangal. The text uses 1420 only. The article names a 'Turkish nobleman' and then says 'Taghalchin was killed'; the text identifies the noble as Taghalchin, as the article implies.
The article gives the rent as '₹3111 per annum'; left out as an anachronistic currency notation.
The article gives the redoubt as 'fifty square feet', which conflicts with the 15 x 20 m size; left out.

The article says the present church 'dates from 1778' but also 'dates from the 13th century'; the text gives only the 1778 form. The Dupplin Cross and Constantín son of Fergus (in the entry) are not in the article.
The article's lead gives the war as 1385–1423 and also says it ran to 1424; the text follows its narrative (withdrawal early in 1424), matching the entry's 1385–1424.

The article gives his life as ca. 232 – 13 January 349; the entry says d. 348. No death date is given in the text. The article says he came from Kucha; the entry says probably Kucha. The text does not restate his origin.
The article gives his birth as 11 March 1861 (and 'born in London in 1861'); the entry's dates say 1862. No birth year is given in the text.

The article gives his birth year as 1539 in the lead and 'about 1534' in the biography; no birth year is given in the text (the entry has c. 1539). The entry says he explored as far as the Sonora region; the article does not mention Sonora.

The article says Corsica became a province of France in 1770; the entry says it did so a few months before Napoleon's birth in 1769. The text gives no date for the province. The article's lead names the Comte de Vaux both as the commander of the first expedition and as the new commander appointed after Borgo; the text names him only at Ponte Novu. The article's lead gives 1769 for Ponte Novu; the entry gives May 1769. The text gives no date.

The entry says their leaders signed protection treaties with Britain in the 1880s; the article places the opposition to the British and the agreement 'at the turn of the 20th century'. The text gives no date for the agreement. Left out: the present Ughaz (named as 'currently'), the Y-DNA section, the long clan tree and the list of modern politicians. The article's claim that the kingdom was 'established more than 600 years ago' is not repeated, as it does not sit easily with the first Ughaz being born in 1575.
The article says Papius was not prominent in the civil wars after the Social War; the entry says he supported the Marians. Left out of the text.

The article says he died 'six years later' after his recall, which does not fit the conquest of Azha in 663 and death in 667 well; the interval is left out and the entry's 667 stands. Tuyunhun is the article's spelling; the entry writes Tuyuhun.
The article quotes George Coedes as holding that Raden Wijaya and Gayatri married before Jayakatwang's revolt; the sentence is garbled ('during which she was killed') and was left out.
The entry says he retired soon after Havana; the article dates his resignation to 1766, given here without 'soon'.

Numbering: the article counts him 14th, also 15th or 16th; the entry says 14th or 15th. Not mentioned in the text. The article calls the Moriarty chieftain the recipient of a reward from Queen Elizabeth after the killing; left out for length.
The entry says he fled after the fall of Gaur and died soon afterwards; the article says he died of wounds received in the siege of Gaur. Both are compatible; no flight is mentioned in the text.

Birth: the article's lead gives c. 1052, its Early life section cites Martin Dimnik for c. 1049; the entry gives no birth year, so none is given here. The Stone of Tmutarakan: the article dates the measurement to the winter of 1067-68, the entry to 1068; left out of the text. Tatishchev's doubtful report of a campaign at Cherson left out.

The article says the dam was completed in 1962; the entry dates it 1963. The completion year is left out. The article gives the lake a length of 56 km; the entry says about 90 km. Length left out. The article says the name was given by 'SardarJi Harbans Singh Somal'; written here as Harbans Singh Somal.
The article's lead says he held the Commonwealth record 'until 1961'; left out as unexplained.

The article's lead says he proclaimed himself king of Shu in 24; its later section places the proclamation while the Xin still faced rebellions. The lead's date is used. The article calls his state the Cheng dynasty and also Chengjia; Chengjia, the entry's name, is used once.

The entry names wars with the settlers in 1856-1857, 1875 and 1910; the article does not mention them, so they are not told here. Left out: the article's reports of brass anklets fed with human blood, rings 'imbued with power via human sacrifice', and the sasswood ordeal with a killing reported in 2025; these rest on unclear sourcing.

The article says 'The first Group Areas Act, the Population Registration Act, 1950'; the Population Registration Act is a separate law, so the first act is described here only by its date of promulgation. Pass laws, mentioned in the article's lead, left out as a separate subject.

The article dates the end of the system to the beginning of the New Order in 1966; the entry gives 1959-1965. The text ends with the 30 September Movement and gives no closing year. Left out for length: the PRRI and Permesta rebellions of 1958 and the CIA's support for them, Operation Trikora, the PKI's land-reform actions, the anti-American campaign of 1964-1965.
SKIPPED: article has about 250 words; it adds little to the description, and its dates for his lands (count in 1016, Champsaur 1027, Oisans 1035) differ from the entry's 'from about 1029'

The article gives two end dates for the war with Samory, 1893 and 1898; the text gives none. The article also speaks of an 'attack on Bamako in 1880' as the trigger of Brière de l'Isle's dismissal, which it elsewhere puts down to the Goubanko raid of 1881; the Goubanko account is used.

The article dates Tell Qanas's occupation to roughly 3700-3100 BC while saying Habuba Kabira South and its acropolis were abandoned after about 120 years; the 3700-3100 span is left out. The article also calls the site 'Bronze Age' though founded in the Late Chalcolithic Uruk period; not repeated.

SKIPPED: article has about 300 words, mostly technical spellings; its radiocarbon date of the 12th century BC for South Arabian letters at Raybun sits uneasily with the entry's early first millennium BCE
